SEO, AEO and GEO Services for Restaurants and Hospitality

Hospitality is the most decision-compressed industry I work in. A diner picks a table in under two minutes, usually one-handed, usually while already moving. A traveller books a room after comparing four options in a single sitting. Neither of them reads a homepage. They read a map result, a rating, an opening-hours line and, increasingly, a paragraph an AI assistant wrote about you.

That means the winning work happens before anyone reaches your website. It happens in the local pack, in structured data, in review signals and in whether a language model can state your cuisine, price range and opening hours without guessing.

Local search decides who gets the booking

Most restaurant discovery ends in the map pack. Three results, ranked on relevance, distance and prominence, with an Open now label doing more persuasive work than any tagline you will ever write. If your hours are wrong on a public holiday, you are not third — you are invisible for that query.

The unglamorous work carries this: a complete and actively maintained Google Business Profile, categories that match how people actually search, service attributes filled in, real photography rather than stock, and name, address and phone details identical everywhere they appear. Conflicting details across directories and aggregators are the single most common reason a well-reviewed restaurant underperforms in maps.

Your menu is data, not decoration

A menu published as a PDF or a flat image is invisible to every system that matters. It cannot be parsed, cannot be quoted, and cannot answer a constrained question like “vegan mains under £15 near me”.

Marked up properly, the same menu becomes an answer. Dish names, prices, cuisine, and dietary attributes such as halal, vegan and gluten-free stop being marketing copy and start being retrievable facts. Combined with Restaurant, Menu and OpeningHoursSpecification schema, that data is what an assistant repeats back to a hungry buyer. Anything you leave unmarked is left to inference, and inference favours whoever documented themselves better.

Reviews are the ranking signal you cannot write yourself

Rating and review volume feed both map rankings and the trust layer that generative engines lean on. What matters is not a one-off push to hit a number, but velocity and recency — a steady flow of recent, specific reviews beats a large pile of old ones.

I set up the asking mechanics so requests land at the moment the guest is happiest, then make sure responses are handled properly. Replying to criticism in public, calmly and specifically, converts better than any five-star average, because prospective guests read how you handle problems.

Multi-location groups and franchises

Groups fail differently from independents. Their problem is rarely visibility for the brand name and almost always cannibalisation between locations, thin duplicated location pages, and profiles managed inconsistently by individual venues.

The fix is architectural: one genuinely distinct page per location with real local content, clean internal linking from a parent hub, consistent naming across every profile, and location-level tracking so you can see which venues are actually pulling demand. This is the same structural discipline covered in my local SEO services, applied at group scale.

Hotels and hospitality: a longer, researched decision

Hotels behave differently from restaurants. The consideration window is longer, the queries are more specific — amenities, proximity to a venue, cancellation terms, family suitability — and third-party platforms occupy much of the results page.

The play is to answer those specific questions on your own pages, in extractable form, so you get quoted directly rather than only through an aggregator that charges commission on the booking. Amenity lists, policy clarity and genuine local guides earn that position.

Being the answer, not just the listing

Answer Engine Optimisation and Generative Engine Optimisation matter more in hospitality than in almost any other vertical, because the queries are naturally conversational. People ask assistants for a quiet restaurant for six on a Friday, or a hotel near a specific venue with late check-out. Those are constraint-filtering questions, and only machine-readable operators qualify for consideration.

My approach here mirrors the method in my AEO and GEO services: make the facts explicit, keep them consistent everywhere, and give independent sources something accurate to corroborate.

What an engagement actually involves

I start by auditing what a search engine and an assistant can currently establish about you — which is often less than owners expect. From there the sequence is access and accuracy first, then structure, then the reputation work that compounds. Technical health underpins all of it; if your pages are slow on a phone on mobile data, nothing else compensates, which is why technical SEO is never optional.

If you want to know what is currently holding your venue back, a free SEO audit is the fastest way to find out.

tabs.tab_title: How is SaaS SEO different from regular SEO?
tabs.tab_content: The intent structure differs. Software buyers search categories, comparisons and alternatives rather than your brand, so coverage of decision-stage queries matters more than publishing volume. SEO, AEO and GEO Services for SaaS and Technology Companies

SaaS buyers do not search the way marketing teams assume. They rarely start with your brand name, and they almost never start with the feature you are proudest of. They start with a problem, then a category, then a shortlist — and by the time your name enters the process, most of the filtering has already happened somewhere you do not control.

That is why product-led SEO for software is less about publishing volume and more about owning the specific queries that decide a shortlist, then making sure an assistant can summarise your product accurately when asked.

The queries that actually decide the deal

Bottom-of-funnel intent in SaaS lives outside your brand. It looks like best [category] software, [competitor] alternatives, [you] vs [competitor], [category] for [role or industry], pricing questions and integration questions.

Each of those needs its own page with its own angle. A single features page cannot serve six different intents, and trying to make it do so is the most common reason technically strong products stay invisible. Comparison and alternative pages in particular feel uncomfortable to write because they name competitors — which is precisely why they convert and why they get cited.

Page architecture that scales without turning into sprawl

The architecture I build for software companies runs on four families: feature pages covering what the product does, use-case pages covering who it is for, integration pages covering what it connects to, and comparison pages covering why you over the alternatives.

Each family targets a different stage of the decision, and each adds entities that strengthen the others. Done properly this compounds; done carelessly it becomes hundreds of thin, templated pages that dilute the site. The dividing line is whether each page answers a question a real buyer asked, in language they used.

Documentation and changelogs are search assets

Most technology companies treat docs as a support cost. In practice, documentation is often the most linked, most cited and most specific content the company owns — developers search error messages, API methods and configuration questions constantly.

If your docs sit behind JavaScript, on a subdomain nobody links to, or in a tool that blocks crawlers, you are discarding your strongest technical authority signal. Making them crawlable, well-structured and internally linked is usually one of the highest-return technical fixes available, and it sits squarely inside technical SEO.

Third-party platforms decide part of your visibility

For software, review platforms and roundups occupy a large share of the results your buyers see. G2, Capterra, industry roundups and community threads frequently outrank vendor sites for category queries, and they are heavily used as sources by generative engines because they read as independent consensus.

You cannot rank a listing you do not own, but you can influence it: keep your category placement and product descriptions accurate, maintain review flow, and make sure the facts on those profiles match your own site exactly. Contradictions between your pricing page and your G2 profile are a trust problem before they are a ranking problem.

Getting recommended inside AI answers

Software evaluation is one of the fastest-moving categories for AI-assisted research. Buyers ask assistants to compare tools, summarise pricing models and recommend options for a stated constraint — team size, budget, compliance requirement, existing stack.

Being included in those answers depends on the same discipline as AEO and GEO anywhere else: state facts explicitly rather than implying them, structure pages so passages can be extracted cleanly, mark up SoftwareApplication and offer data, and ensure independent sources corroborate what you claim. Vague positioning language is invisible to a retrieval system.

Measuring what matters in SaaS

Sessions are a poor proxy for a business that sells subscriptions. I report on qualified signups and trials from organic, assisted conversions across the longer research path, and share of visibility on the specific comparison and category queries that precede a purchase.

I also run a fixed panel of buying prompts through the major assistants each month and log whether the product is mentioned and how it is described. When a model gets your pricing model or integration list wrong, that is a content gap you can fix — and it is usually costing you deals silently.

Where I would start

Almost always with coverage and structure rather than volume. I map the category, find which decision-stage queries have no page behind them, fix the technical issues blocking crawl and render, then build the missing pages in order of commercial value. Semantic SEO holds it together, keeping the whole site legible as one coherent subject rather than a pile of feature copy.

If you want a clear read on which decision-stage queries you are currently absent from, start with a free SEO audit.

tabs.tab_title: Should filtered category URLs be indexed?
tabs.tab_content: Only where there is genuine search demand and unique inventory behind them — brand, size, colour and material usually qualify. Sort order, page size, session parameters and arbitrary price bands should not be indexable, because they reorder the same products without creating anything new.

tabs.tab_title: What should happen to out-of-stock products?
tabs.tab_content: It depends on whether the product returns. Seasonal items should stay live with accurate availability status. Permanently discontinued items should redirect to the nearest equivalent or the parent category — never in bulk to the homepage, which is treated as a soft 404.

tabs.tab_title: Does Shopify or WooCommerce rank better?
tabs.tab_content: Neither has an inherent advantage. Both can rank extremely well and both create predictable problems — Shopify with its URL structure and collection handling, WooCommerce with performance and plugin bloat. Platform choice matters far less than how the catalogue is structured.

tabs.tab_title: Can my products appear in AI shopping answers?
tabs.tab_content: If your data is complete and consistent, yes. Assistants filter on price, availability, shipping and returns, so those fields must be explicit in structured data and identical across your site and any merchant feeds. Anything only stated in an image is invisible.

SEO, AEO and GEO Services for E-commerce and Retail

An online store is the hardest kind of site to keep technically clean. It generates URLs faster than anyone can review them, its inventory changes daily, and the pages that matter most commercially are usually the ones templated the most cheaply. Most stores I audit are not losing to better content — they are losing to their own URL sprawl.

The work splits into three parts: make the catalogue crawlable and coherent, make each product legible as structured data, and make sure the store still gets recommended when the buyer asks an assistant instead of typing a query.

Category pages earn the rankings, product pages close the sale

Most non-branded demand lands on categories, not products. “Merino wool coats” is a category query; “SKU 4471 in navy, size M” is not. Yet categories are usually the thinnest pages on the site — a heading, a grid, and pagination.

A category page that ranks needs a reason to exist beyond listing products: buying guidance, the distinctions that matter in that category, the questions people ask before choosing. That content also feeds answer engines, which quote explanation far more readily than a product grid.

Faceted navigation is where crawl budget goes to die

Filters are the single most destructive pattern in retail SEO. Four filters with five options each generate hundreds of combinations, and if every combination is crawlable you have quietly created more URLs than you have products.

The decision is per-parameter, not global. Facets with genuine search demand and unique inventory — brand, size, colour, material — deserve indexable, linkable URLs with their own titles. Facets that only reorder the same items — sort order, page size, session identifiers, arbitrary price bands — should never be indexable. Getting this wrong is the most common reason a large store's important pages are crawled infrequently.

Product data has to be complete, not just present

Marking up a product with a name and an image is close to useless. The fields that decide whether you appear in a rich result or a generated comparison are the commercial ones: price, availability, aggregateRating, gtin, shipping details and return policy.

Those same fields feed shopping surfaces and merchant feeds, so the work pays twice. One rule I hold to on every build: structured data must match the visible page exactly. A feed that says in stock while the page says sold out is a trust problem, and it is the kind of inconsistency that quietly removes a store from consideration.

Out-of-stock and discontinued products

Retail sites accumulate dead URLs faster than any other type. The instinct is to delete them in bulk, which throws away every link and ranking signal those pages earned.

Seasonal products that will return should stay live with clear availability status. Permanently discontinued items should redirect to the closest equivalent or the parent category — never to the homepage, which search engines treat as a soft 404. Handled well, a retired product keeps working for you; handled badly, it is a slow leak.

Reviews and user-generated content

Reviews do three jobs at once in retail: they corroborate your claims, they cover long-tail phrasing you would never think to target, and they keep product pages fresh without anyone writing anything. Questions and answers on product pages do the same, and often answer the exact objection blocking the sale.

Collect them honestly and mark them up accurately. Review markup that does not match visible reviews is a shortcut that ends badly.

Getting recommended by assistants

Shopping research has moved quickly into conversational tools. Buyers ask for options under a budget, in a material, that ship within a week and can be returned free. Those are constraint filters, and only stores whose data is machine-readable qualify.

This is the same discipline as my AEO and GEO work: state the facts explicitly, keep them identical everywhere, and give independent sources something accurate to agree with. If your delivery window lives only in an image on a banner, it does not exist.

Where I start

Almost always with crawl and index health, because on a store that is where the compounding damage sits. Then category depth, then product data completeness, then the reputation layer. Platform matters less than people expect — the same principles apply on Shopify, WooCommerce or a custom stack, though each has its own quirks, which is why I also handle the development side rather than handing over a document.

If you want to know how many URLs your filters are really generating, a free SEO audit will show you.

tabs.tab_content: On any page making clinical claims, yes — named, credentialled, with a visible review date. Purely practical pages such as parking, opening hours or fees do not need clinical review, but they still need to be accurate and attributable to the organisation.

tabs.tab_title: Can we ask patients for reviews?
tabs.tab_content: Within the rules of your regulator, generally yes, but the process needs care. Ask consistently at an appropriate point in care rather than selectively, never incentivise, and never disclose anything identifying in a public response — acknowledge and move the conversation offline.

tabs.tab_title: How do we handle multiple clinic locations?
tabs.tab_content: Each location needs a genuinely distinct page with real local detail — practitioners, access, transport, parking — plus its own claimed and maintained Google Business Profile. Templated pages with only the town name changed compete with each other and rarely rank.

SEO, AEO and GEO Services for Healthcare and Clinics

Healthcare is the one vertical where getting SEO wrong has consequences beyond revenue. Search engines classify medical content as “Your Money or Your Life” and hold it to a visibly higher standard, which means the shortcuts that work elsewhere actively hurt here.

It is also the vertical where the gap between how clinics write and how patients search is widest. Patients search symptoms in plain language. Clinics publish service names in clinical language. Bridging that gap, credibly, is most of the work.

Patients search the problem, not your service

Nobody wakes up searching for a procedure by its clinical name. They search what they are feeling, in their own words, often phrased as a question and often at two in the morning.

That means condition and symptom pages are the entry point, and service pages are the conversion point. A clinic site built only around services is invisible for the searches that actually start the journey. The structure I build reflects the patient's sequence: what is wrong with me, how is it treated, who treats it, and where do I go.

E-E-A-T is not optional in health content

Every health page needs to answer three questions immediately: who wrote this, what qualifies them, and who checked it. “Written by our team” fails all three, and a language model cannot verify it either.

Practically: a named clinician with visible qualifications, a linked practitioner profile, a named medical reviewer with a visible review date, and cited sources or guideline references for clinical claims. Add the organisational trust layer — registration numbers, clear pricing, a contactable address, a complaints policy — and you have the specification search engines describe in their quality guidelines.

This is the strictest application of the E-E-A-T principles I apply everywhere, and in health it is the difference between ranking and being suppressed.

Careful claims are a ranking advantage

There is a strong temptation in clinic marketing to promise outcomes. Beyond the regulatory risk, overstated claims are a visibility risk: content that promises certainty where medicine offers probability reads as untrustworthy to reviewers and to models trained on clinical literature.

Accurate, hedged, well-sourced writing genuinely performs better here. Saying that most patients recover within a stated range, with a caveat about individual variation, outperforms a confident guarantee — and it is the version a careful clinician would sign off.

Local visibility decides who gets the appointment

Almost all healthcare demand is local and urgency-weighted. Someone in discomfort chooses on proximity, availability and confidence, in that order.

So the local layer carries enormous weight: a complete Google Business Profile per site, accurate opening hours including holidays, correct practitioner listings, and consistent name, address and phone details everywhere. Multi-site groups need genuinely distinct location pages with real local detail — practitioners, access, parking, transport — not one template with the town name swapped. That structural work is covered in my local SEO services.

Reviews, handled with care

Review signals matter as much in healthcare as anywhere, but the constraints are tighter. Patient confidentiality limits what you can say in a public response, and you cannot solicit or curate reviews the way a restaurant can.

What works is a compliant, consistent request process at the right point in care, and responses that acknowledge without ever disclosing. A calm, non-defensive reply to a negative review does more for a prospective patient than a perfect average, because they are reading how you behave under pressure.

Being cited by assistants, accurately

Patients now ask assistants about symptoms constantly, and those tools are deliberately conservative with health information — they favour sources with clear authorship, institutional credibility and verifiable citations.

That works in favour of clinics that do the trust work properly. Structure your content so a clear answer sits immediately under a question-shaped heading, mark up MedicalOrganization, Physician and FAQPage where appropriate, and keep every clinical claim attributable. My AEO and GEO work applies the same method, just with a higher evidence bar.

How an engagement runs

I start by auditing trust signals and local accuracy, because those are usually the binding constraints. Then the content architecture — condition, treatment and location pages — followed by the technical foundation, which in healthcare tends to matter for accessibility as much as ranking: many patients are older, on slower connections, or using assistive technology.

If you want an honest read on how a search engine currently assesses your clinic's credibility, a free SEO audit is the place to start.

SEO, AEO and GEO Services for Real Estate

Property websites have a structural problem no other industry shares: most of their content expires. A listing is live for a few weeks, earns links and rankings, then sells — and the usual response is to delete it. Do that a few thousand times and you have systematically destroyed the authority the site spent years accumulating.

The fix is to build the layer that lasts. Listings bring traffic; area pages, guides and property-type pages are the asset that compounds.

Area pages are the real estate SEO asset

Buyers and renters search places before they search properties. “Family areas near [town]”, “2-bed flats in [area]”, “is [neighbourhood] a good place to live”. Those queries have consistent volume, no expiry date and very little serious competition, because most agencies pour everything into listings.

A genuine area page is not a paragraph of filler above a property grid. It answers what living there is actually like: transport links, schools, price trends, who the area suits, how it compares to the neighbouring one. That content earns links naturally, gets quoted by assistants answering relocation questions, and keeps working long after today's listings are gone.

What to do when a listing sells

This single decision separates property sites that compound from ones that reset every year.

A sold listing still answers a real question — what did that property go for, what does this street trade at. Keep it live with a clear sold status and a link back to the area page, or redirect it to the closest relevant page. What you must not do is bulk-delete thousands of URLs into 404s, because every link and every ranking signal disappears with them. If the page must go, redirect it to the area or property-type page, never to the homepage.

Listings need to be crawlable in the first place

Many property portals and agency sites load listings through JavaScript, behind map interfaces or infinite scroll. If a crawler cannot reach a listing without executing a search, that listing effectively does not exist.

Every property needs a stable, linkable URL reachable through normal navigation — not only through a map widget. Paginated, crawlable index pages by area and property type solve this cleanly. It is unglamorous technical SEO, and on property sites it is usually the highest-value fix available.

Local presence and agent credibility

Property is a high-value, trust-heavy decision made locally. Sellers in particular choose an agency on perceived local dominance and credibility.

That makes the local layer decisive: a complete Google Business Profile per branch, consistent details everywhere, genuine local content rather than templated town pages, and individual agent profiles that resolve as real people with real track records. Agent profiles are consistently underused — people search for named agents, and a proper profile page captures that demand while strengthening the entity signals around the brand. The structural side is covered in my local SEO services.

Reviews and vendor confidence

A seller choosing between agencies is comparing evidence, not adjectives. Review volume and recency feed map rankings, and detailed reviews mentioning specific areas and outcomes do double duty by reinforcing local relevance.

Ask consistently after completion, respond to everything, and surface the results where vendors are deciding — on valuation and branch pages, not buried on a testimonials page nobody visits.

Structured data for property

Property markup is less standardised than retail, but the fundamentals still apply. Mark up the organisation and each branch as a RealEstateAgent with accurate location data, use Residence or Product patterns for listings where appropriate, and mark up agent profiles as people with verifiable roles.

Keep the visible page and the markup identical. A listing marked available while the page says under offer is exactly the inconsistency that gets a source quietly discounted.

Getting recommended by assistants

Relocation research suits conversational tools unusually well. People ask which area fits a budget, which neighbourhood suits families, what the commute is really like. These are judgement questions, and assistants answer them from sources that offer genuine local knowledge.

Agencies that publish genuine area knowledge get cited. Those publishing thin location pages built for keywords do not. It is the same principle as my AEO and GEO work: be the source worth quoting.

Where I start

With crawlability and the listing lifecycle, because that is where the recurring damage is. Then the area page layer, then agent profiles and the local presence. If you want to know how much authority your sold listings have taken with them, a free SEO audit will quantify it.
